laws.title: Bangladeshi Culture — Islam, Hospitality and Humility
laws.subtitle: Right hand, respectful address, dress modestly
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh is a predominantly Muslim country. Similar to Pakistan: use right hand, greet with Assalam-o-Alaikum, dress modestly especially outside major cities. Always remove shoes before entering homes. Accept offered tea/food. Elder respect is paramount — use 'Bhai' (brother) or 'Apa' (sister) with slight age differences; 'Uncle/Aunty' for older people.
laws.penalty: Not legal — disrespecting religious customs or elders causes significant social offence.
exceptions: Dhaka has a more cosmopolitan business culture

quiz.q: What respectful term do Bangladeshis use for someone slightly older?
quiz.explanation: 'Bhai' (brother) and 'Apa' (sister) are used as respectful terms for people slightly older in Bangladeshi culture.

laws.title: Drug Laws — Extremely Harsh Penalties
laws.subtitle: Narcotics Control Act 1990 — Death penalty for trafficking
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh has extremely harsh drug laws. Drug trafficking carries a mandatory death penalty. Possession of even small amounts of cannabis or other drugs can result in imprisonment. The Narcotics Control Act 1990 is strictly enforced. Dhaka and Cox's Bazar are areas where drug enforcement is active. 'Yaba' (methamphetamine tablet) is a major enforcement priority — arrests are frequent.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: death penalty or life imprisonment. Possession (any amount): 2–10 years imprisonment. Cannabis: 2–5 years for possession.
exceptions: Medical prescriptions for licensed substances
No practical tolerance for recreational use

quiz.q: What is the maximum penalty for drug trafficking in Bangladesh?
quiz.explanation: Drug trafficking in Bangladesh carries the death penalty under the Narcotics Control Act 1990 — one of the world's harshest drug laws.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Laws — Criminal Under Penal Code Section 377
laws.subtitle: Penal Code §377 — Up to life imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh criminalises same-sex relations under Penal Code Section 377 (inherited from British colonial law), with penalties of up to life imprisonment. In practice, prosecutions under 377 are less common than harassment, extortion, and violence from police and others. Bangladesh has a recognised 'third gender' (hijra community) with official government ID, creating a complex legal landscape.
laws.penalty: Same-sex relations: up to life imprisonment under §377. In practice: police harassment, extortion, and arbitrary detention are more common.
exceptions: Third gender (hijra) community has limited official recognition
No formal enforcement exceptions

quiz.q: Bangladesh's Penal Code Section 377 carries a maximum penalty of?
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's §377 carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment for same-sex relations, though prosecutions are less common than police harassment.

laws.title: Traffic Laws — Left-Side Driving; Rickshaw and CNG Culture
laws.subtitle: Road Transport Act — Left side; 0.00% BAC zero tolerance
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh drives on the left (British legacy). Dhaka is one of the world's most congested cities — notorious traffic is a fact of daily life. Cycle rickshaws (non-motorised) and CNGs (auto-rickshaws) are the primary local transport in Dhaka. Bus overtaking, lane violations, and pedestrian priority are generally not observed in practice. Drink driving is technically zero tolerance (0.00% BAC) given the overwhelmingly Muslim population. Seatbelts are mandatory. Driving in Bangladesh requires an international driving permit.
laws.penalty: Drink driving (any amount): criminal offence. No IDP: vehicle confiscation. Accidents in Bangladesh: scene can be dangerous — crowds gather quickly.
exceptions: None for drink driving limit

quiz.q: Which side of the road does Bangladesh drive on?
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh drives on the left — a legacy of British colonial rule, along with India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and most of South Asia.

laws.title: Plastic Bag Ban — First Country to Ban Polythene Bags
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh Environment Protection Act 1995 — Nationwide polythene ban since 2002
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh was the first country in the world to ban plastic polythene bags, doing so in 2002 after devastating floods were made worse by plastic bags clogging drainage systems. The ban covers manufacturing, marketing, and use of polythene bags below 55 microns. Despite patchy enforcement, the law remains in force and Bangladesh has become a global model for plastic bag legislation. Single-use plastics face increasing restrictions. Jute bags (Bangladesh is the world's largest jute producer) are the promoted alternative.
laws.penalty: Manufacturing or selling banned polythene bags: up to 10 years imprisonment or fines up to BDT 10 lakh (approx USD 9,000); enforcement is inconsistent in practice
exceptions: Bags above 55 microns thickness are technically permitted
Medical and industrial packaging exemptions

quiz.q: Bangladesh made history in 2002 by becoming the first country in the world to do what?
options: Mandate solar panels on all buildings
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh banned polythene bags in 2002 — the world's first nationwide plastic bag ban — after devastating floods showed how plastic blocked drainage systems.

laws.title: Digital Security Act — Social Media Criticism of Government Leads to Arrests
laws.subtitle: Digital Security Act 2018 — Up to 14 years for online 'false or offensive' content
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Digital Security Act (DSA) 2018 criminalises a wide range of online speech, including content deemed to 'spread confusion', 'tarnish the image of the state', or 'hurt religious sentiments'. The Act was widely condemned by press freedom organisations — Reporters Without Borders called it 'a tool of repression'. Journalists, bloggers, cartoonists, and ordinary Facebook users have been arrested under it, including for sharing satirical posts about the Prime Minister. In 2023, the DSA was replaced by the Cyber Security Act (CSA) which retained many of the same provisions despite promises of reform. Bangladesh is regularly listed among the world's most repressive countries for online speech.
laws.penalty: Publishing 'false, obscene or defamatory' information: up to 3 years + BDT 3 lakh fine. Attacking 'liberation war spirit' or religious sentiment: up to 7 years. Cyberattacks on critical infrastructure: up to 14 years.
exceptions: Journalism with editorial oversight is theoretically protected but enforcement has targeted journalists anyway
Academic publications with institutional backing
laws.sourceLabel: Digital Security Act 2018 — Bangladesh Ministry of Law

quiz.q: What replaced Bangladesh's Digital Security Act in 2023?
options: No replacement — it was simply repealed
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh replaced the Digital Security Act with the Cyber Security Act (CSA) in 2023, but critics noted the new law retained most of the same restrictive provisions despite promised reforms.

laws.title: Minority Religious Restrictions — Hindu Temples and Buddhist Sites Require Care
laws.subtitle: Religious sites protection — but minority communities face vulnerability
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh is a Muslim-majority country (around 90%) with significant Hindu, Buddhist and Christian minorities. While the constitution guarantees religious freedom, periodic communal violence against Hindu and Buddhist communities occurs — particularly around elections or when religious offence is alleged. Visitors should dress modestly at all religious sites, remove shoes at temples and mosques, and ask permission before photographing worshippers. The Hindu festival of Durga Puja and Buddhist Rakhain communities in Cox's Bazar have specific ceremonial protocols. Photographing the military, government buildings, or Rohingya refugee camps requires official media accreditation.
laws.penalty: Photography of military or refugee camps without accreditation: detention and camera confiscation. Religious insult under Section 28 of the Digital Security Act: up to 7 years.
exceptions: Accredited journalists with press cards
Approved humanitarian workers with UNHCR/NGO credentials
Religious ceremonies: most welcome visitors who observe protocols
laws.sourceLabel: Human Rights Watch — Bangladesh Religious Freedom Report

quiz.q: What percentage of Bangladesh's population is Muslim?
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh is approximately 90% Muslim, with significant Hindu, Buddhist and Christian minorities protected in theory by the constitution.

laws.title: Climate Vulnerability — Flooding, Cyclones and Disaster Zone Entry Rules
laws.subtitle: DDM — Red zone flooding: evacuation orders are mandatory and legally binding
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh is one of the world's most climate-vulnerable countries — approximately one-third of the country floods annually, and the Bay of Bengal cyclone season (April–May and October–November) regularly brings deadly storms. The Department of Disaster Management (DDM) issues mandatory evacuation orders for coastal and river-prone areas during cyclones and major floods. Ignoring evacuation orders is a criminal offence under Bangladesh's Disaster Management Act 2012. Tourists and visitors in coastal areas (Cox's Bazar — the world's longest natural beach) must register at local police stations and follow evacuation directives. The Sundarbans mangrove delta (UNESCO World Heritage) has controlled entry zones that close during cyclone conditions.
laws.penalty: Ignoring mandatory evacuation order: criminal offence under Disaster Management Act 2012 — fine + possible detention for non-compliance. Re-entering a closed zone: up to 2 years.
exceptions: Emergency services and disaster response personnel with authorisation
UN and humanitarian agencies with disaster coordination accreditation

quiz.q: Under Bangladesh's Disaster Management Act 2012, what is the status of mandatory evacuation orders?
options: Legally binding — ignoring one is a criminal offence
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's Disaster Management Act 2012 makes mandatory evacuation orders legally binding — ignoring one during a cyclone or major flood can result in a fine or detention, reflecting the serious life-safety stakes.

laws.title: Rickshaw Art and Jamdani Weaving — Bangladesh's UNESCO Cultural Heritage
laws.subtitle: UNESCO Intangible Heritage — Jamdani muslin: protected craft; rickshaw art tradition
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh has two UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage listings: Jamdani weaving (2013) — the extraordinarily fine muslin weaving tradition of the Dhaka region — and Mangal Shobhajatra (2016), the colourful procession held on Bengali New Year (Pohela Boishakh, April 14). Jamdani muslin was historically so fine it was called 'woven air' — British colonial-era policies devastated the industry, but it has been revived. Authentic Jamdani must be woven manually on handlooms; machine-woven imitations are misrepresented as Jamdani. The colourful rickshaw art tradition (hand-painted imagery on cycle rickshaws) is a distinctive cultural form being documented as heritage. Pohela Boishakh celebrations on April 14 are a major national celebration with specific festival protocols.
laws.penalty: Mislabelling machine-made fabric as authentic Jamdani: consumer fraud offence under Trade Marks Ordinance 2009. Disrupting Pohela Boishakh processions: public order offence.
exceptions: Certified Jamdani weavers with Bangladesh Handloom Board registration
Academic documentation of rickshaw art traditions
laws.sourceLabel: UNESCO — Jamdani Weaving: Bangladesh Intangible Cultural Heritage

quiz.q: What was the poetic name given to the extraordinarily fine Dhaka Jamdani muslin that was historically woven in Bangladesh?
quiz.explanation: Dhaka muslin — especially Jamdani — was historically called 'woven air' (or 'woven wind') because it was so fine that a full sari could pass through a finger ring. The British colonial period devastated the industry, but Jamdani weaving was revived and is now UNESCO-listed.

laws.title: Garment Factory Safety Laws — Rana Plaza Aftermath and ACCORD/Alliance Reforms
laws.subtitle: 2013 Rana Plaza collapse killing 1,134 triggered global supply chain safety regulations
laws.fullDescription: The April 2013 collapse of Rana Plaza garment factory near Dhaka — killing 1,134 workers — became the deadliest industrial accident in the history of the garment industry. It triggered unprecedented global reform: the Accord on Fire and Building Safety (signed by 200+ European brands) and the Alliance for Bangladesh Worker Safety (North American brands) created binding inspection regimes for Bangladeshi factories supplying major retailers. Bangladesh Labour (Amendment) Act 2013 expanded workers' rights to organize. The Bangladesh National Building Code was updated. By 2018, 1,600+ factories were inspected and hundreds of structural issues remediated. The post-ACCORD Bangladesh Sustainability Compact with EU, US, and Bangladesh committed to ongoing monitoring. Bangladesh's garment sector employs 4 million workers (80% women) and represents 80% of export earnings.
laws.penalty: Factory owners violating safety standards: fines up to BDT 25,000 (~$230) under Labor Act (widely criticized as insufficient). Criminal negligence in industrial accidents: up to 4 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Export Processing Zones (EPZs) have a separate regulatory framework (EPZ Labour Act)
Informal home-based garment work outside formal factory regulation
Foreign-branded buyers operating under voluntary Accord/Alliance standards rather than government law
laws.sourceLabel: Bangladesh Accord on Fire and Building Safety

quiz.q: How many workers were killed in the 2013 Rana Plaza garment factory collapse in Bangladesh?
quiz.explanation: The Rana Plaza collapse on April 24, 2013 killed 1,134 workers and injured 2,500 more — making it the deadliest industrial accident in garment industry history. The disaster prompted the creation of the binding Accord on Fire and Building Safety, signed by over 200 international brands.

laws.title: 2024 Student Revolution — Sheikh Hasina's Ouster and Quota Reform Protests
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's student movement toppled PM Hasina in August 2024 over civil service quota discrimination
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's July–August 2024 protests began over civil service job quotas that reserved 30% of government positions for descendants of 1971 Liberation War fighters — a system critics called discriminatory nepotism. Student protests turned into a mass movement against PM Sheikh Hasina's 15-year rule. Security forces killed 300+ protesters. Hasina fled to India on August 5, 2024, ending the Awami League's decade-and-a-half in power. A caretaker government under Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus took over. The Supreme Court reduced the quotas to 5% (7% for other groups, 93% merit-based). Bangladesh faces a democratic transition: outstanding human rights cases against Hasina's government, economic stabilization after the disruption, and reconstruction of institutions politicized under her rule.
laws.penalty: The protests were a political movement — student demonstrators faced criminal charges for riot, sedition, and murder. Hasina faces criminal charges in Bangladesh related to the crackdown.
exceptions: Caretaker government created a transition framework for prosecution of crackdown perpetrators
International criminal justice mechanisms being considered for the most serious cases

quiz.q: What specific government policy triggered Bangladesh's 2024 student uprising that eventually toppled PM Hasina?
options: A university tuition fee increase of 400%
Civil service quotas reserving 30% of positions for descendants of 1971 Liberation War fighters
A crackdown on student unions at Dhaka University
Mandatory military service for university graduates
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's 2024 uprising began over civil service quota reform — specifically quotas reserving 30% of government positions for descendants of 1971 Liberation War fighters. Students argued this was discriminatory nepotism that blocked merit-based advancement. The movement expanded into a broader anti-Hasina revolution that resulted in her resignation and exile.

laws.title: Student Uprising Ousts Sheikh Hasina
laws.subtitle: 2024 quota reform protests toppled 15-year autocratic government in days
laws.fullDescription: In July–August 2024, Bangladesh experienced one of the most dramatic political uprisings in Asia's recent history. What began as student protests against a quota system reserving 30% of government jobs for descendants of 1971 Liberation War fighters spiraled into a nationwide revolution after security forces killed hundreds of protesters. Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who had ruled autocratically for 15 years — suppressing opposition, rigging elections, and using enforced disappearances — fled to India on August 5, 2024 as crowds stormed her official residence. Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was appointed to lead an interim government.
laws.penalty: During protests: hundreds killed by police and ruling Awami League's student wing. Criminal charges filed against Hasina in absentia for crimes against humanity. Opposition BNP members released from prison.
exceptions: Interim government operating without elected mandate — constitutional questions remain
Bangladesh's constitution requires elections within 90 days of dissolution though this timeline was extended
Yunus government's mandate comes from military backing and popular legitimacy, not constitution

quiz.q: What triggered the student protests that ultimately toppled Sheikh Hasina's government in Bangladesh in 2024?
options: A quota reserving 30% of government jobs for Liberation War descendants
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's 2024 revolution began as protests against a quota reserving 30% of government jobs for descendants of the 1971 Liberation War fighters, which students saw as discriminatory — but grew into a broader uprising against Hasina's 15-year autocracy after security forces killed hundreds of protesters.

laws.title: Rana Plaza Collapse & Garment Safety Reform
laws.subtitle: 1,134 workers killed in 2013 building collapse transformed global fashion industry safety standards
laws.fullDescription: On April 24, 2013, the Rana Plaza garment factory complex in Dhaka collapsed, killing 1,134 workers — the deadliest garment factory disaster in history. Workers had reported cracks in the building the day before but were forced to return. The tragedy prompted the Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh — signed by 200+ global fashion brands — requiring independent inspections of over 1,600 factories, mandatory remediation, and workers' right to refuse unsafe work. Bangladesh also reformed its Labour Act. The Accord saved an estimated 150+ lives through remediation of safety hazards. An updated International Accord continues operations as a permanent safety body.
laws.penalty: Factory owners who force workers into unsafe conditions: criminal negligence charges, up to 3 years imprisonment under Bangladesh Labour Act. Non-remediation of flagged hazards: brands face supply chain termination under Accord.
exceptions: Export processing zones (EPZs) have separate labour regulations with different enforcement mechanisms
Small factories under 50 workers have reduced inspection frequency
Factories supplying only domestic market are outside the Accord's scope
laws.sourceLabel: International Accord for Health and Safety in the Textile and Garment Industry

quiz.q: How many workers were killed in the 2013 Rana Plaza garment factory collapse in Bangladesh?
quiz.explanation: The April 2013 Rana Plaza collapse killed 1,134 workers — the deadliest garment factory disaster in history — prompting the Accord on Fire and Building Safety signed by 200+ global fashion brands to independently inspect and remediate factory safety hazards.

laws.title: 2024 Student Revolution & Fall of Sheikh Hasina
laws.subtitle: Student protests over job quotas toppled a 15-year government in a historic popular uprising
laws.fullDescription: In July–August 2024, Bangladesh experienced a student-led revolution that overthrew Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, ending 15 years of Awami League rule. The protests began over a quota system reserving 30% of civil service jobs for descendants of 1971 liberation war veterans, which students called discriminatory. When security forces and Awami League paramilitaries attacked protesters — killing over 300 — the movement expanded into a demand for Hasina's resignation. On August 5, 2024, Hasina fled to India by helicopter. Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was sworn in as head of an interim government. The quota system was subsequently abolished by the Supreme Court.
laws.penalty: Participants in the protests faced charges of vandalism and murder; most were released under the interim government. Former Awami League officials face ongoing prosecutions
exceptions: The Supreme Court ruling abolished the controversial quota system before Hasina's fall
Yunus government suspended many politically motivated cases filed under the previous administration

quiz.q: What triggered Bangladesh's 2024 student revolution that ultimately toppled Sheikh Hasina?
options: A proposed quota reserving civil service jobs for liberation war descendants
quiz.explanation: The revolution began over a quota system reserving 30% of civil service jobs for descendants of 1971 liberation war veterans. When security forces killed protesters, the movement expanded into a full uprising that ousted PM Sheikh Hasina.

laws.title: Dhaka's Air Quality Crisis: World's Most Polluted Capital City
laws.subtitle: Dhaka regularly tops global air pollution rankings — and Bangladesh's environmental enforcement remains critically weak despite laws on the books
laws.fullDescription: Dhaka, Bangladesh's capital of 22 million, regularly ranks as the world's most air-polluted city by AQI (Air Quality Index) measurements. Bangladesh's Environment Conservation Act (1995) and Environment Conservation Rules (1997) theoretically regulate industrial emissions, brick kilns, and vehicle emissions. In practice, enforcement is minimal: thousands of illegal brick kilns surround Dhaka, burning coal and old tires; rickshaws and two-stroke engines fill the air with particulates; and construction dust is unregulated. The Bangladesh Environment Court (established 2010) hears environmental cases but lacks investigative capacity. WHO estimates air pollution causes 80,000+ deaths annually in Bangladesh.
laws.penalty: Industrial pollution violations: fines of BDT 10,000–1,000,000 (~$90–$9,000) and closure orders. Repeat violations: imprisonment up to 2 years. In practice, enforcement actions are rare
exceptions: Export processing zones have slightly different industrial standards
Emergency directives have temporarily shut brick kilns during major pollution crises

quiz.q: Approximately how many deaths does the WHO estimate air pollution causes annually in Bangladesh?
quiz.explanation: The WHO estimates air pollution causes over 80,000 deaths annually in Bangladesh — making it one of the country's leading preventable killers, closely linked to Dhaka's status as one of the world's most polluted cities.

laws.title: Rana Plaza Building Code Law
laws.subtitle: Post-2013 collapse: strict structural safety codes for garment factories
laws.fullDescription: The 2013 Rana Plaza building collapse killed over 1,100 garment workers and became a global symbol of industrial negligence. Bangladesh responded with the Bangladesh National Building Code (BNBC) amendments and mandatory factory inspections under the National Tripartite Plan of Action. Factory owners must obtain structural certificates, and the Accord on Fire and Building Safety (now the International Accord) conducts independent audits. Employers who force workers into structurally unsafe buildings face criminal charges under the Labour Act 2006 amendments.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years imprisonment and heavy fines for factory owners; factory closure orders
exceptions: Buildings with up-to-date structural certificates are exempt from mandatory closure
International Accord inspections can grant provisional compliance status
laws.sourceLabel: International Accord on Health and Safety in the Textile Industry

quiz.q: How many workers died in the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse?
quiz.explanation: The Rana Plaza building collapse on April 24, 2013 killed over 1,100 people, making it the deadliest garment-factory disaster in history.

laws.title: Climate Refugee Legal Framework
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's law addresses displacement from sea-level rise and flooding
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh is one of the world's most climate-vulnerable countries — approximately one-third of its land can flood annually, and sea-level rise threatens to inundate 17% of its coastal territory by 2050. Bangladesh's Delta Plan 2100 is a comprehensive government framework for climate adaptation, embedding environmental considerations into all major planning decisions. The Bangladesh Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan (BCCSAP) guides domestic policy, while Bangladesh has been a leading voice at UNFCCC negotiations for a 'Loss and Damage' fund (established at COP27 2022). Bangladesh has over 3 million internal climate migrants, and the Bangladesh Supreme Court has recognized climate change as a human rights threat.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a policy and planning framework; violations of environmental regulations within it carry administrative fines
exceptions: Delta Plan 2100 implementation is phased and funding-dependent
laws.sourceLabel: Bangladesh Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

quiz.q: What percentage of Bangladesh's coastal territory could be submerged by sea-level rise by 2050?
quiz.explanation: Current projections suggest that approximately 17% of Bangladesh's coastal territory could be permanently inundated by sea-level rise by 2050, displacing tens of millions of people in what would be one of history's largest climate displacements.

laws.title: Cyclone Preparedness System
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's cyclone warning system has saved hundreds of thousands of lives
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Cyclone Preparedness Programme (CPP), established in 1972 after a 1970 cyclone killed 300,000 people, is now recognized as one of the world's best disaster early warning systems. Bangladesh's Disaster Management Act 2012 and Standing Orders on Disasters (SOD) create legal frameworks for government disaster response. The CPP deploys 55,000 trained volunteers who operate 2,000 coastal shelters. Bangladesh reduced cyclone deaths from 300,000 in 1970 to under 200 in comparably powerful storms in 2007 and 2009. The achievement has been studied globally as a model for disaster risk reduction.
laws.penalty: Local government officials who fail to implement evacuation orders: administrative sanctions and potential criminal liability for gross negligence
exceptions: Vulnerable populations (elderly, disabled) receive special assisted evacuation provisions

quiz.q: How many deaths did Bangladesh's 1970 cyclone cause, compared to under 200 in comparably powerful recent storms?
quiz.explanation: The 1970 Bhola Cyclone killed approximately 300,000 people in Bangladesh (then East Pakistan). By contrast, Cyclone Sidr (2007) and Cyclone Aila (2009) — of similar intensity — killed fewer than 200 people each, demonstrating the success of Bangladesh's preparedness system.

laws.title: Garment Industry Labor Laws and Rana Plaza Legacy
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's 2013 factory collapse prompted global supply chain reform and worker safety laws
laws.fullDescription: The collapse of Rana Plaza on April 24, 2013 — a garment factory building in Savar near Dhaka that killed 1,134 workers — was the deadliest garment factory disaster in history and triggered a global reckoning over fast fashion supply chains. In response, Bangladesh amended its Labor Act (2006) with the 2013 Bangladesh Labor (Amendment) Act and created new regulations: factory structural inspections became mandatory; fire safety, building safety, and electrical safety standards were raised; workers gained the right to form trade unions without prior approval (partially); and the Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh and the Alliance for Bangladesh Worker Safety were formed — international frameworks between global brands and trade unions for factory inspections. The minimum wage for garment workers was raised multiple times (most recently to 12,500 taka/month in 2023). Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China.
laws.penalty: Factory owners violating safety standards: fines up to 25,000 taka and/or 1 year imprisonment; repeat violations: license revocation and criminal prosecution; labor law violations: civil penalties
exceptions: Export Processing Zones (EPZs) have a separate labor framework with some restrictions on union formation
Small garment factories below 25 workers have simplified compliance requirements

laws.title: Student Revolution and Fall of Sheikh Hasina (2024)
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's 2024 student protests toppled Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina after 15 years in power
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh experienced a dramatic political revolution in July-August 2024. Student protests initially targeted a Supreme Court ruling that partially reinstated a controversial 30% quota reserving government jobs for descendants of 1971 independence war freedom fighters. The quota system was seen as unfair and benefiting the ruling Awami League party's support base. The government's violent crackdown — with police and Awami League student wing (BCL) using live ammunition, killing over 200 protesters — transformed the quota protests into a broader anti-government movement. On August 5, 2024, Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina resigned and fled to India. Military chief General Waker-Uz-Zaman addressed the nation, and Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was appointed head of an interim government. The Awami League, in power since 2009, was comprehensively removed. The episode followed years of concerns about democratic backsliding under Hasina. Bangladesh's constitution, courts, and legal institutions faced a comprehensive transition.
laws.penalty: Former government officials face prosecution for ordering use of force against protesters; Awami League leaders arrested on multiple charges; former BCL members faced community violence
exceptions: The new interim government operated under a constitutional framework despite unclear legal basis
International students and foreigners were protected during the transition
Garment industry operations continued under emergency protocols to protect export revenues

laws.title: Sheikh Hasina Ousted by Student Uprising
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's 15-year ruler fled as a student revolution ended her government
laws.fullDescription: In August 2024, a student-led uprising toppled Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina after weeks of protests that began against a quota system for government jobs. The movement expanded into a broader pro-democracy revolution against Hasina's increasingly autocratic 15-year rule. When security forces killed hundreds of protesters, the military withdrew its support and Hasina fled to India. Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was asked to lead an interim government. The uprising brought down a government that had won elections widely seen as rigged, jailed opposition leaders including BNP chief Khaleda Zia, and presided over enforced disappearances. Bangladesh's transition faced enormous political and economic challenges.
laws.penalty: Crimes against protesters: murder charges filed against Hasina and officials. Internet shutdown orders: administrative measure used during crisis now subject to legal challenge.
exceptions: Interim government has limited mandate — cannot make permanent constitutional changes
Hasina's location in India complicated extradition as India has no extradition treaty with Bangladesh

quiz.q: What initially triggered the 2024 Bangladesh student uprising that ousted Sheikh Hasina?
options: Protests against a quota system for government jobs that expanded into a pro-democracy revolution
A military coup that students opposed
Economic collapse caused by garment factory closures
quiz.explanation: The uprising began as protests against a quota system reserving government jobs for descendants of 1971 independence fighters, then expanded into a broader pro-democracy revolution after security forces killed protesters.

laws.title: Muhammad Yunus Leads Interim Government After Hasina's Fall
laws.subtitle: Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus became Bangladesh's interim leader after the student revolution
laws.fullDescription: After Sheikh Hasina's flight from Bangladesh in August 2024, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus — founder of Grameen Bank and microcredit pioneer — was asked by the student movement to lead an interim government. Despite being 84 years old, Yunus accepted and was sworn in as Chief Adviser. His government faced enormous challenges: restoring judicial independence, conducting fair elections, managing a fragile economy with high inflation and external debt, and prosecuting Hasina-era human rights abuses. Yunus sought to rebuild Bangladesh's democratic institutions while facing pressure from Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) seeking quick elections. International support flowed from the US and Western democracies.
laws.penalty: Hasina-era repression crimes: prosecuted under Bangladesh's existing criminal law framework. Corruption from previous government: prosecuted by newly reformed Anti-Corruption Commission.
exceptions: Transitional justice framework being developed — some political prisoners from Hasina era released
Interim government has limited mandate for constitutional reform — elections required for permanent changes

quiz.q: For what achievement is Muhammad Yunus, Bangladesh's interim leader, most internationally known?
options: Negotiating Bangladesh's independence from Pakistan in 1971
Founding Grameen Bank and pioneering microcredit lending, which won him the Nobel Peace Prize
Leading Bangladesh's delegation at the Paris Climate Agreement
Running Bangladesh's largest NGO for 30 years
quiz.explanation: Muhammad Yunus won the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize for founding Grameen Bank and developing the microcredit model — small loans to impoverished entrepreneurs (primarily women) without collateral — a concept that spread globally and revolutionized development finance.

laws.title: Bangladesh Garment Industry Labor Regulations
laws.subtitle: Post-Rana Plaza reforms transformed global supply chain standards
laws.fullDescription: The 2013 Rana Plaza building collapse killing 1,134 garment workers triggered massive reforms to Bangladesh's labor laws and factory safety standards. The Bangladesh Accord on Fire and Building Safety (now the International Accord) established legally binding safety inspections in garment factories. The Bangladesh Labour Act was amended to expand trade union rights, improve safety standards, and require compensation for injured workers. Brands sourcing from Bangladesh must ensure supplier compliance. The minimum wage was raised to BDT 12,500/month (~$113) in 2024.
laws.penalty: Factory safety violations: fines up to BDT 5 million and closure orders. Prohibiting trade union formation: fines up to BDT 25,000 and imprisonment up to 2 years. Child labor: fines up to BDT 10,000 per child plus imprisonment
exceptions: Export Processing Zones (EPZs) have separate labor rules with some restrictions on unions
Informal sector workers have different and weaker protections
Home-based piece workers have limited coverage
laws.sourceLabel: Bangladesh Ministry of Labour and Employment

quiz.q: What event triggered major labor law reforms in Bangladesh in 2013?
options: The Rana Plaza building collapse killing 1,134 workers
quiz.explanation: The collapse of the Rana Plaza garment factory building in 2013, killing 1,134 workers, triggered sweeping reforms to Bangladesh's labor laws, factory safety standards, and international supply chain accountability measures.

laws.title: Bangladesh's Sheikh Hasina Ouster and Revolution
laws.subtitle: 2024 student uprising ends Sheikh Hasina's 15-year rule
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's July-August 2024 student uprising, initially triggered by protests against a quota system for government jobs, escalated into a mass uprising that forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to flee the country on August 5, 2024 after at least 300 people were killed in crackdowns. An interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus took power. Mass looting and attacks on Awami League offices followed. The interim government arrested and charged Hasina in absentia with crimes against humanity. Bangladesh's Awami League was effectively banned from operating. Major constitutional and electoral reforms were announced.
laws.penalty: Sheikh Hasina (in absentia): crimes against humanity, murder charges for protest killings — potential life imprisonment or death penalty. Awami League members: mass arrests for corruption and violence. Security forces who fired on protesters: investigations and prosecutions announced
exceptions: International law protects Hasina as long as she remains in India (which has not extradited her)
Interim government decrees operate outside normal legislative procedures under state of emergency provisions

laws.title: Digital Security Act Repeal and Cyber Security Act

Academic commentary with appropriate framing

laws.title: Bangladesh Climate Vulnerability and Adaptation Laws

The Bay of Bengal Climate Accord

laws.title: Delta Plan 2100

Traditional bamboo construction below certain heights has simplified building rules
Agricultural structures in floodplains have modified requirements

laws.penalty: Labor law violations subject to factory shutdowns and fines
exceptions: Export processing zone different regulations
Skill-based wage differentials

quiz.q: What sector employs the majority of Bangladesh's industrial workforce?
quiz.explanation: Garment manufacturing employs approximately 4 million workers and accounts for over 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings.

laws.title: Climate Migration and Managed Retreat
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh Plans Systematic Coastal Relocation
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh, one of the world's most climate-vulnerable countries, developed systematic policies for managing climate migration from coastal and flood-prone areas. The government created climate resilience hubs in safer locations and developed pathways for workers to migrate internationally. Bangladesh became a global model for managed climate adaptation.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; voluntary relocation programs
exceptions: Compensation for displaced households
Livelihood transition support

quiz.q: What makes Bangladesh particularly vulnerable to climate change?
options: Low-lying delta geography prone to flooding and sea level rise
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's low-lying Ganges-Brahmaputra delta geography makes it extremely vulnerable to sea level rise and intensifying monsoon flooding driven by climate change.

laws.title: Pharmaceutical Industry and Generic Drug Export
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh Becomes Major Generic Medicine Exporter
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh developed a significant generic pharmaceutical manufacturing industry, benefiting from LDC status that exempted it from TRIPS intellectual property agreements until 2033. Bangladeshi generic medicines supplied African and other developing country markets at low prices. The industry faced challenges as Bangladesh graduated from LDC status.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; quality control and GMP compliance
exceptions: LDC TRIPS waiver ongoing
Quality certification requirements for export

quiz.q: What international agreement exemption helped Bangladesh develop its pharmaceutical industry?
options: TRIPS intellectual property waiver for LDC countries
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh benefited from a TRIPS intellectual property waiver for Least Developed Countries until 2033, allowing generic drug manufacturing without paying patent royalties.

laws.title: Garment Industry Diversification Beyond Fast Fashion
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh upgrades from low-cost apparel to higher-value manufacturing
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter, with the sector employing 4 million workers (80% women). Following the 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse that killed 1,100+ workers, safety standards have dramatically improved. Bangladesh now seeks to diversify beyond low-margin fast fashion into technical textiles, pharmaceuticals, and electronics. The country upgraded many factories to green building standards, with more LEED-certified garment factories than any other country.
laws.penalty: Factories violating safety standards face closure orders, fines, and loss of export certification
exceptions: Small enterprises under 50 workers have graduated compliance timelines
Export processing zones have separate regulatory frameworks

laws.title: Student Revolution and Sheikh Hasina's Fall
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's quota protests topple 15-year Hasina government
laws.fullDescription: In July-August 2024, student protests against a quota system reserving government jobs for descendants of 1971 liberation war fighters escalated into a full revolution. After security forces killed hundreds of protesters, the movement demanded and achieved Sheikh Hasina's resignation. She fled to India after 15 years in power. A caretaker government under Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus took power. The revolution demonstrated that mass civic action could remove an apparently entrenched authoritarian government. Elections and constitutional reform are pending.
laws.penalty: The quota system that triggered protests was struck down; new merit-based hiring implemented
exceptions: Disabled persons and minorities retain separate quota provisions for inclusion
Special quotas for tribal communities in the Chittagong Hill Tracts maintained

quiz.q: Who leads Bangladesh's caretaker government after Hasina's fall?
quiz.explanation: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, founder of Grameen Bank and microcredit pioneer, was asked to lead Bangladesh's interim government after Sheikh Hasina fled following the student-led revolution.

laws.title: Sea Level Rise and Delta Nation Survival
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh faces existential threat as Ganges-Brahmaputra delta sinks
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh sits on one of the world's largest river deltas, with 80% of the country as low-lying floodplain. Sea level rise, cyclone intensification, and river flooding create compounding threats. The Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta is also subsiding from sediment compaction and groundwater extraction. Bangladesh invests in 5,000+ km of embankments, cyclone shelters, and early warning systems that have dramatically reduced cyclone deaths. The country is also adapting agriculture to saline intrusion with salt-tolerant rice varieties.
laws.penalty: Construction in coastal embankment zones requires flood assessment and elevated foundation requirements
exceptions: Traditional char island farming communities have different land use provisions
Government cyclone shelter construction exempt from normal procurement timelines for emergency builds

quiz.q: What percentage of Bangladesh is low-lying floodplain?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 80% of Bangladesh consists of low-lying floodplain on the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta — making it extraordinarily vulnerable to sea level rise, cyclones, and river flooding.

laws.title: Jute Revival and Eco-Textile Opportunity
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's golden fiber jute returns as sustainable packaging boom
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh produces 80% of the world's jute — a natural fiber once displaced by plastic packaging. The global shift away from single-use plastics has revived interest in jute bags, packaging, and textiles as sustainable alternatives. Bangladesh is developing premium jute products including geotextiles for erosion control and jute composites for automotive interiors. Government research has developed golden jute varieties with higher yield and fiber quality. Jute offers Bangladesh diversification beyond garments.
laws.penalty: Jute exporters must meet quality grading standards for international markets
exceptions: Small farmer jute producers can sell through government depots without individual certification
Value-added jute products have different export documentation than raw fiber

quiz.q: Why is jute experiencing a revival after decades of decline?
options: Lower production costs than synthetic alternatives
Global shift away from single-use plastics creating demand for natural fiber packaging
quiz.explanation: The global shift away from single-use plastics has revived demand for jute — a completely natural, biodegradable fiber — for bags, packaging, and other applications where plastic is being phased out.

laws.title: Sheikh Hasina Overthrow and Student Revolution
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's dramatic political transition through mass protests
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's long-serving Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina was dramatically ousted in August 2024 by a student-led mass protest movement that began over a job quota system. The protests against reserving 30% of civil service jobs for descendants of 1971 independence war veterans escalated into a broader uprising after security forces killed hundreds of protesters. Hasina fled to India, and Nobel Peace Prize winner Muhammad Yunus was asked to lead an interim government. The movement, primarily driven by students and young people, was remarkable for its leaderless and decentralized organization through social media. Bangladesh's economy, primarily powered by garment exports making it the world's second-largest apparel exporter, faces political uncertainty during the transition.
laws.penalty: Protest-related deaths are being investigated; former officials face potential accountability measures
exceptions: The interim government operates under different legal authority than a normal elected government

quiz.q: What initially triggered the student protests that led to Sheikh Hasina's ouster?
options: Demand for elections after alleged fraud
Opposition to a quota reserving 30% of civil service jobs for war veterans' descendants
quiz.explanation: The protests began over a quota system reserving 30% of civil service positions for descendants of 1971 independence war veterans. When security forces killed protesters, the demonstrations escalated into a broader uprising that ousted Prime Minister Hasina.

laws.title: Climate Frontline Nation and Managed Displacement
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh losing land to sea level rise while housing millions
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh is one of the world's most climate-vulnerable countries — a low-lying river delta where 80% of the land is flood-prone and rising sea levels threaten the Sundarbans mangrove forest (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) and the livelihoods of millions of coastal residents. The country already manages some of the world's highest internal climate migration, with millions moving from coastal and flood-prone areas to cities, particularly Dhaka. The Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100 is one of the world's most comprehensive long-term water and delta management strategies, developed with Dutch expertise. Bangladesh has achieved remarkable reductions in extreme poverty, maternal mortality, and child malnutrition despite its geographic and economic constraints. The country has been an active voice in international climate negotiations and has used its population of 170 million living in a small area to dramatize the human cost of climate inaction.
laws.penalty: Coastal zone regulations restrict certain development in hazard areas; building codes carry permit requirements
exceptions: Some traditional agricultural and fishing communities have historic rights to use coastal and deltaic lands

quiz.q: What percentage of Bangladesh's land is flood-prone?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 80% of Bangladesh's land is flood-prone, making it one of the world's most climate-vulnerable countries and driving the Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100 as one of the most comprehensive long-term water management strategies ever developed.

laws.title: Student Revolution Ousts Sheikh Hasina
laws.subtitle: Quota protest becomes uprising ending 15-year autocracy
laws.fullDescription: Sheikh Hasina's 15-year rule ended in August 2024 when a student-led revolution swept her from power after weeks of protests against quota systems in government jobs. The movement began with university students protesting job reservation quotas for descendants of 1971 liberation war freedom fighters. When the government violently cracked down, the protests transformed into a broader uprising. Hasina fled to India, and a Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus-led interim government took power.
laws.penalty: Former officials facing corruption and crackdown accountability investigations; Hasina government supporters prosecuted
exceptions: Interim government has limited legislative authority; major laws require elected parliament
International human rights standards apply to accountability process

quiz.q: Who leads Bangladesh's interim government after Sheikh Hasina's ouster?
quiz.explanation: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus was chosen to lead Bangladesh's interim government after Sheikh Hasina fled to India following the student revolution of August 2024.

laws.title: Garment Industry Safety Post-Rana Plaza
laws.subtitle: Decade of reform after deadliest factory collapse
laws.fullDescription: The 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse that killed over 1,100 garment workers triggered the most significant global supply chain safety reform in history. Western brands signed binding accord agreements requiring independent safety inspections. A decade later, factory conditions have improved dramatically but remain imperfect. Bangladesh's garment industry employs over 4 million workers—mostly women—and generates 80% of export earnings. The industry faces new challenges from automation, fast fashion changes and competition from lower-wage countries.
laws.penalty: Fire and building safety standards enforced through Accord inspection regime; brands sourcing from non-compliant factories face public accountability
exceptions: Small factories below worker threshold have different regulatory regime
Emergency safety orders can halt production at dangerous facilities

quiz.q: How many workers were killed in the 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh?
quiz.explanation: The 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh killed over 1,100 garment workers, making it the deadliest industrial accident in the garment industry's history and triggering major global supply chain safety reforms.

laws.title: Digital Bangladesh and IT Export Growth
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh builds tech sector alongside garment manufacturing
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Digital Bangladesh initiative, championed by the Hasina government before her ouster, aimed to transform the country's economy through ICT development. Dhaka has developed a significant software and IT services export sector alongside the dominant garment industry. The country has trained hundreds of thousands of IT workers and established software technology parks. Bangladesh competes with India and Pakistan for outsourced IT work. The mobile banking system bKash, partnered with BRAC bank, has been a global model for mobile financial services reaching the unbanked.
laws.penalty: ICT companies operating in designated software technology parks receive tax exemptions; data protection regulation being developed
exceptions: Export-oriented IT companies receive VAT and tax incentives
Bangladesh Software and Information Services Association members benefit from advocacy support

quiz.q: What is the name of Bangladesh's mobile banking platform that became a global model for financial inclusion?
quiz.explanation: bKash, a mobile banking platform partnered with BRAC Bank in Bangladesh, became a global model for reaching unbanked populations with financial services through mobile phones—one of the world's most successful mobile financial inclusion stories.

laws.title: RMG Sector and Economic Transformation
laws.subtitle: Garment manufacturing drives Bangladesh's middle-income transition
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's ready-made garment (RMG) sector represents over 80% of export earnings and employs over 4 million workers, predominantly women. The sector drove Bangladesh from least-developed to lower-middle income status. Bangladesh has used garment exports to build foreign reserves, invest in education and reduce poverty dramatically. The challenge is moving up the value chain—developing design, branding and higher-value manufacturing beyond basic assembly. Bangladesh aims to reach upper-middle income status by 2031.
laws.penalty: Labor law requires minimum wage, overtime limits and factory safety standards; brands sourcing from Bangladesh face supply chain due diligence requirements
exceptions: Export processing zones have modified labor regulations affecting organizing rights
Small factories below threshold have simplified compliance requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association

quiz.q: What percentage of Bangladesh's export earnings does the garment sector represent?
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's ready-made garment sector represents over 80% of export earnings and employs over 4 million workers—the foundation of Bangladesh's economic transformation from least-developed to lower-middle income status.

laws.title: Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100 and Climate Change Strategy
laws.subtitle: Racing Against Rising Seas
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100 and its Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan (BCCSAP) address one of the world's most severe climate vulnerabilities. Bangladesh is extremely flat — 80% below 10 meters elevation — and densely populated with 170 million people. Sea level rise, cyclones, river flooding, and saltwater intrusion threaten millions of climate refugees. The Sundarbans — the world's largest mangrove forest, shared with India — is shrinking. Bangladesh has been a leading voice for climate justice and Loss and Damage finance at COP negotiations, despite contributing less than 0.5% of global emissions.
laws.penalty: Environment Conservation Act fines; environmental courts; criminal penalties for major violations
exceptions: Informal urban settlements under adapted building standards
Traditional fishing and agriculture

laws.title: Bangladesh Essential Services Package
laws.subtitle: BRAC and Community Health Workers
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh provides an Essential Service Package through its public health system, covering primary and preventive care. Bangladesh has achieved remarkable health progress with limited resources — dramatically reducing child and maternal mortality, controlling cholera, and achieving high vaccination coverage. A major driver is BRAC (originally Bangladesh Rural Advancement Committee) — the world's largest NGO — which operates millions of community health workers providing basic health education and services. Bangladesh pioneered oral rehydration therapy (ORS) which has saved millions globally. However, significant challenges remain in hospital quality and non-communicable diseases.
laws.penalty: Health facility licensing required; drug safety enforcement by DGDA; criminal liability for quacks and unlicensed practice
exceptions: Traditional herbal medicine practitioners under separate licensing
Community health workers operate in simplified regulatory framework

laws.title: Bangladesh Garment Worker Rights Post-Rana Plaza
laws.subtitle: Fashion Industry's Deadliest Disaster
laws.fullDescription: The April 24, 2013 Rana Plaza garment factory collapse in Bangladesh killed 1,134 workers — the world's deadliest industrial accident in decades. The disaster transformed global apparel supply chain accountability. The Accord on Fire and Building Safety (now the International Accord) required major brands to fund and implement independent safety inspections across Bangladesh's 4,500+ garment factories. Bangladesh amended its Labor Act to allow union registration without employer consent. Bangladesh's RMG (Ready-Made Garments) industry employs 4+ million workers, 80% women, and accounts for 85% of exports.
laws.penalty: Factory safety violations: Department of Inspection for Factories; labor violations: labor courts; Accord signatory brands jointly liable for safety
exceptions: Export Processing Zone workers under separate EPZ Labor Act
Home-based workers largely outside formal framework

laws.title: National Education Policy 2010
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's education overhaul and free textbook program
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's National Education Policy 2010 standardized a two-stream system: general education and madrassa education. Bangladesh's Textbook Festival (পাঠ্যপুস্তক উৎসব) distributes free textbooks to all primary and secondary students on January 1 annually—a massive logistical achievement distributing 350+ million books. Female enrollment has achieved near parity at primary level due to stipend programs. However, 2024-2025 saw curriculum controversies following political changes, with the interim government revising textbooks.
laws.penalty: Schools not participating in free textbook distribution programs face ministry penalties; private schools must register and meet curriculum standards
exceptions: English medium schools follow different curricula
Madrassa stream follows modified curriculum integrating religious and secular education

quiz.q: Bangladesh's annual 'Textbook Festival' distributes free textbooks to students on what date?
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh distributes free textbooks to all primary and secondary students on January 1 each year in a program called Pathyapoosto Utsob (Textbook Festival), distributing over 350 million books annually.

laws.title: Rohingya Refugee Crisis and Labor Emigration
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's dual role as refugee host and labor exporter
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh hosts approximately 1 million Rohingya refugees from Myanmar's Rakhine State following the 2017 military crackdown. The world's largest refugee camp (Cox's Bazar) houses 900,000+ in extremely crowded conditions. Bangladesh has prevented Rohingya from integrating — restricting movement, work, and education — hoping for eventual repatriation. Simultaneously, Bangladesh is a major labor exporter: 10+ million Bangladeshis work abroad (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Malaysia, Singapore) sending $21 billion in annual remittances. The Wage Earners Welfare Board protects overseas workers.
laws.penalty: Rohingya refugees found outside Cox's Bazar camps may be returned to camps; local Bangladeshis assisting unauthorized Rohingya movement face prosecution; recruitment agencies violating worker standards face license suspension
exceptions: UNHCR-registered Rohingya receive minimal legal protections
Bangladeshi workers in Gulf countries are covered by bilateral labor agreements
laws.sourceLabel: Bangladesh Foreign Minister Policy and UNHCR Bangladesh

quiz.q: Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh hosts approximately how many Rohingya refugees, making it the world's largest refugee camp?
quiz.explanation: Cox's Bazar in southeastern Bangladesh hosts over 900,000 Rohingya refugees, primarily those who fled Myanmar's military crackdown in 2017, making it by far the world's largest refugee settlement.

laws.title: Narcotics Control Act
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's drug law and yaba methamphetamine crisis
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Narcotics Control Act criminalizes drug trafficking and use strictly. Bangladesh faces a severe yaba (methamphetamine tablets mixed with caffeine, from Myanmar) epidemic, particularly among youth. Yaba trafficking from Myanmar through Bangladesh has been growing for years. Bangladesh's Department of Narcotics Control (DNC) conducts major operations. Drug trafficking can result in the death penalty. Under Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina (until 2024), a 'war on drugs' resulted in many extrajudicial killings similar to the Philippines. The Yunus interim government (2024+) has reviewed these policies.
laws.penalty: Personal drug use: up to 6 months; drug trafficking: 2 years to death; large-scale trafficking: death penalty; manufacturing drugs: death penalty; trafficking to minors: enhanced penalties
exceptions: Drug users may be diverted to treatment facilities
Medical narcotics by prescription
First-time small possession offenders may receive diversion

quiz.q: Bangladesh faces a severe epidemic of yaba — a methamphetamine-caffeine tablet manufactured primarily in which neighboring country?
quiz.explanation: Yaba (Thai for 'crazy drug') tablets are primarily produced in Myanmar's Shan State by militias and ethnic armed groups. They are smuggled into Bangladesh (and Thailand) in massive quantities, driving youth drug addiction and organized crime growth.

laws.title: Section 377 Criminalizes Same-Sex Conduct
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh maintains British-era penal code criminalizing homosexuality with up to life imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh retains Section 377 of its Penal Code, inherited from British colonial rule, which criminalizes 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature.' The penalty is 10 years to life imprisonment. LGBTQ+ individuals face severe social stigma and state harassment. In 2014, Bangladesh launched an official hijra (third gender) category on passports and national ID cards, providing a form of legal recognition for a traditional third gender community. However, LGBTQ+ organizations cannot operate openly, and foreign LGBTQ+-rights advocacy has faced government pushback.
laws.penalty: Same-sex conduct is punishable by 10 years to life imprisonment under Section 377
exceptions: Official hijra third-gender category recognized on government documents

quiz.q: Bangladesh criminalizes same-sex conduct under Section 377. What unique LGBTQ+-related step did Bangladesh take in 2014?
quiz.explanation: In 2014, Bangladesh created an official hijra third-gender category on passports and national IDs, recognizing a traditional South Asian third gender community — a rare legal acknowledgment amid criminalization of same-sex conduct.

laws.title: Digital Security Act Targets Journalists
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's Digital Security Act has been weaponized against journalists and critics
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Digital Security Act (DSA) of 2018 has been widely used to imprison journalists, bloggers, and critics. The law imposes up to 14 years imprisonment for content deemed defamatory, 'spreading rumors,' or 'offensive to religious sentiments' online. Under PM Sheikh Hasina (until her 2024 removal), journalists were routinely arrested under the DSA. Bangladesh has also used the Information and Communication Technology Act (ICTA) against media. Local journalists covering corruption and political violence face physical danger. The transitional government post-2024 has promised reforms. Self-censorship is widespread.
laws.penalty: Digital Security Act: up to 14 years imprisonment for online content; journalists face physical violence and legal harassment
exceptions: Post-Hasina transitional government has pledged DSA reform

quiz.q: What did Bangladesh's Digital Security Act of 2018 impose on journalists for certain online content?
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's Digital Security Act (2018) imposes up to 14 years imprisonment for online content deemed defamatory, 'spreading rumors,' or offensive to religious sentiments — a provision widely used against journalists and critics under the Hasina government.

laws.title: Digital Security Act and Social Media Censorship
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's DSA has been used to prosecute social media users and block platforms
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Digital Security Act (DSA) 2018 criminalizes online content deemed defamatory, offensive to religious sentiments, or spreading rumors — with imprisonment up to 14 years. The DSA has been widely used against social media users, bloggers, and journalists. During the 2024 protests against Sheikh Hasina that led to her removal, Bangladesh shut down mobile internet and blocked Facebook, YouTube, and other platforms. Bangladesh's BTRCr (Bangladesh Telecom Regulatory Commission) controls platform access. After Hasina's removal, a transitional government pledged DSA reform. Meta has removed some government-requested content.
laws.penalty: DSA: up to 14 years imprisonment for digital content offenses; platforms blocked during political crises
exceptions: Post-Hasina transitional government pledged reforms to the DSA

quiz.q: What digital actions did Bangladesh take during the 2024 protests that led to Hasina's removal?
options: Shut down mobile internet and blocked Facebook and YouTube
quiz.explanation: During the 2024 mass protests against Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh shut down mobile internet access and blocked platforms including Facebook and YouTube — digital censorship measures that ultimately failed to prevent the protests that forced Hasina from power.

laws.title: Bangladesh Bank Crypto Ban & MFS Mobile Money Rules
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh bans crypto while leading South Asia in mobile financial services
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh Bank (BB) issued a circular in 2014 declaring cryptocurrency transactions illegal under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act and Money Laundering Prevention Act. This ban remains in force. Despite this, Bangladesh has achieved remarkable financial inclusion through Mobile Financial Services (MFS) — bKash (owned partly by BRAC Bank) handles over 250 million transactions monthly with 75 million users. BB's regulations strictly govern MFS providers' capital requirements, transaction limits, and agent banking rules. Bangladesh also has an extensive agent banking network serving rural populations. Remittances (over $21 billion annually) are a critical source of foreign exchange.
laws.penalty: Cryptocurrency transactions: violators face prosecution under Foreign Exchange Regulation Act with fines or imprisonment up to 5 years; AML violations: imprisonment up to 12 years
exceptions: Licensed money transfer operators handling remittances have different FX rules
Agent banking in rural areas has simplified KYC for accounts under BDT 200,000
Islamic banking products have modified accounting standards

quiz.q: What Bangladesh mobile financial service has over 75 million users and processes hundreds of millions of transactions monthly?
quiz.explanation: bKash, backed by BRAC Bank and Alibaba affiliate Ant Financial, is Bangladesh's dominant mobile financial service with over 75 million registered users — representing a major financial inclusion success story in a country of 170 million.

laws.title: BFSA Food Safety Authority & Formalin-Contaminated Fish Crisis
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh fights widespread food adulteration including formalin in fish and fruit
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Bangladesh Food Safety Authority (BFSA) was established in 2015 to consolidate food safety regulation. Bangladesh has a severe food adulteration crisis: investigations have repeatedly found formalin (formaldehyde solution, a preservative used for corpses) in fish and tropical fruits to extend shelf life and improve appearance. Other common adulterations include artificial ripening of fruits with calcium carbide (illegal but widespread), adulterated spices, and substandard edible oil. Bangladesh's large informal food sector — street food, small restaurants — operates largely outside formal oversight. The BFSA has limited enforcement capacity relative to the scale of the market. Bangladesh has specific export certification for its growing shrimp export industry (world's top 5 shrimp exporters).
laws.penalty: BFSA food adulteration violations: fines up to BDT 5 lakh and imprisonment up to 5 years; formalin use in food: specific mobile court penalties; export certification fraud: export ban
exceptions: Traditional home food preparation is unregulated
Agricultural direct sales to local markets have simplified BFSA requirements
Religious charitable food distribution (iftar during Ramadan) has modified rules

quiz.q: What illegal chemical preservative has been repeatedly found in fish and fruits in Bangladesh markets?
options: Boric acid added to keep prawns firm
Formalin (formaldehyde solution) used to extend shelf life and improve appearance
Bleaching agents added to make fish appear fresher
Industrial dyes added to make fruits more colorful
quiz.explanation: Formalin (formaldehyde solution) — normally used for preserving corpses and tissue samples — has been repeatedly found in fish and tropical fruits sold in Bangladeshi markets. It extends shelf life and maintains appearance but is highly toxic and carcinogenic. Mobile courts and BFSA inspections target formalin use as a major public health priority.

laws.title: Bangladesh Animal Welfare — Limited Formal Framework
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh lacks comprehensive animal welfare law; cruelty provisions are minimal
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh has no comprehensive national animal welfare law. Animal welfare is addressed through the Cruelty to Animals Act, 1920 (inherited from British India) and some veterinary regulations. The 1920 Act has outdated penalty structures — fines of a few hundred taka — and limited scope. Bangladesh has significant working animal populations (including working cattle and horses in urban transport). Dhaka and other cities have significant stray dog populations, managed through periodic culling campaigns rather than sterilization. Animal fighting is practiced in some rural areas. Bangladesh is also a transit country for illegal wildlife trafficking. Growing urban middle class interest in companion animals is slowly building advocacy for stronger legal protections.
laws.penalty: Cruelty to Animals Act 1920: minimal fines equivalent to a few USD; no imprisonment; largely unenforced
exceptions: Livestock farming
Halal slaughter
Traditional animal husbandry
Fishing

quiz.q: What framework does Bangladesh primarily use for animal welfare regulation?
options: The colonial-era Cruelty to Animals Act 1920 with minimal updates
A regional SAARC animal welfare treaty
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh still relies primarily on the colonial-era Cruelty to Animals Act 1920 inherited from British India — a law with minimal penalties (a few hundred taka) and very limited scope. No comprehensive modern animal welfare legislation has been enacted.

laws.title: Bangladesh Muslim Family Laws Ordinance and Dowry Law
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh criminalizes dowry demands and protects women in divorce
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh largely follows the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (inherited from Pakistan's union and applicable to Muslim majority). Bangladesh has also enacted the Dowry Prohibition Act (1980, amended 2018) — which criminalizes demanding or giving dowry, a practice that has been linked to domestic violence and 'dowry deaths.' Bangladesh's Family Courts Ordinance 1985 established dedicated family courts handling divorce, maintenance, custody, and dower. Women can seek divorce through khula or fasakh. The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 set 18 for girls and 21 for boys as minimum marriage ages (but with a controversial 'special circumstances' exception without minimum age for girls). Bangladesh has domestic violence provisions under the DVP Act 2010.
laws.penalty: Dowry demands: up to 5 years imprisonment; child marriage facilitation: imprisonment and fines; non-payment of mehr: civil enforcement; domestic violence: protective orders and imprisonment
exceptions: 'Special circumstances' exception to minimum marriage age for girls (criticized)
Non-Muslim personal laws apply to minorities
Hindu customary practices in some areas
laws.sourceLabel: Bangladesh Family Courts Ordinance 1985 & Muslim Family Laws Ordinance

quiz.q: What controversial exception exists in Bangladesh's Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017?
options: Boys under 15 can marry with parental consent
A 'special circumstances' exception allows girls under 18 to marry without specifying a minimum age
Marriages between cousins are exempt from age requirements
Religious marriages are exempt from the minimum age
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 set 18 as the minimum marriage age for girls but included a controversial 'special circumstances' exception allowing marriages of girls below 18 in certain circumstances — without specifying a lower age limit. Critics argued this undermined the law's protective intent and could enable child marriage.

laws.title: Bangladesh Registration Act & Property Rights
laws.subtitle: Land administration and vested property issues
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's property law is based on the colonial Transfer of Property Act (1882) and Registration Act (1908). A major historical issue is the Vested Property Act (Enemy Property Act 1965, renamed 1974), which allowed the government to seize property of Hindus who migrated to India during 1965 war and 1971 Liberation War, depriving millions of their land. The Vested Properties Return Act (2011) began a process of returning properties. Land disputes are extremely common in Bangladesh; the court system is backlogged with millions of cases. The Digital Land Management System is being developed to address record-keeping issues.
laws.penalty: Property abandonment without due process: court challenge available; vested property reclaim: administrative application
exceptions: Vested Property Return Act 2011 still being implemented
Land disputes account for majority of court cases in Bangladesh
laws.source: Transfer of Property Act 1882; Vested Properties Return Act 2011

quiz.q: What communities were primarily affected by Bangladesh's 'Vested Property' (Enemy Property) Act?
options: Muslims who moved to West Pakistan
Hindu minorities who migrated to India during conflicts
quiz.explanation: The Enemy Property Act (1965, later renamed Vested Property Act) allowed seizure of properties of Hindus who migrated to India during 1965 and 1971, depriving millions of minority community members of their land in what is now Bangladesh.

laws.title: Bangladesh Consumer Rights Protection Act 2009
laws.subtitle: Consumer rights with directorate enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Consumer Rights Protection Act (2009) established the Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection (DNCRP) as the enforcement agency. The Act prohibits adulteration of food and goods, false advertising, overcharging, and anti-consumer behavior. Mobile courts (under the Mobile Court Act 2009) conduct on-the-spot inspections of markets and can impose instant fines for price gouging and adulteration. Consumer associations are active, particularly during Ramadan when price monitoring intensifies. Bangladesh's rapid garment industry growth has led to specific consumer-side issues around counterfeit products. Digital financial services (mobile banking) consumer protections are overseen by Bangladesh Bank.
laws.penalty: DNCRP fine: up to BDT 200,000; mobile courts: instant fines for market violations; adulteration: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Mobile courts conduct on-the-spot market enforcement
Ramadan price monitoring is a major annual consumer protection activity
laws.source: Consumer Rights Protection Act 2009; Mobile Court Act 2009

quiz.q: What enforcement mechanism allows Bangladesh authorities to fine market vendors on the spot?
options: Mobile Courts under the Mobile Court Act 2009
DNCRP inspection squads with fining power
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's Mobile Court Act (2009) authorizes magistrates to conduct on-the-spot inspections and impose immediate fines for violations like price gouging, adulteration, and short weights — a rapid enforcement mechanism that allows swift action in markets without lengthy court proceedings.

laws.title: Constitution of Bangladesh, 1972
laws.subtitle: People's Republic established after liberation war from Pakistan
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Constitution (1972) was adopted one year after independence from Pakistan following the 1971 Liberation War (Mukti Yuddho) in which 300,000-3,000,000 people were killed and 10 million fled to India as refugees. The Constitution declares Bangladesh a 'People's Republic' with four fundamental principles: nationalism, socialism, democracy, and secularism ('Mujibism'). After PM Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's assassination (1975), subsequent governments removed 'socialism' and 'secularism', adding 'absolute trust in Almighty Allah'. The 15th Amendment (2011) under Sheikh Hasina (Mujib's daughter) restored secularism but kept Islamic references — Bangladesh is officially secular with Islam as state religion, a constitutional paradox.
laws.penalty: Challenging the state's constitutional foundations: sedition provisions under Penal Code. Presidential emergency (Article 141A) suspends rights.
exceptions: Fundamental rights enforceable by High Court through writ jurisdiction
Bangladesh has abolished preventive detention without trial after transitional period
Constitutional amendments require two-thirds majority — recently more controlled under Awami League

quiz.q: How many people died in Bangladesh's 1971 Liberation War from Pakistan?
options: An estimated 300,000 to 3,000,000 — a genocide whose exact toll remains contested
15 million — virtually the entire population was affected
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's 1971 Liberation War is one of history's most contested genocides in terms of death toll: Bangladesh officially claims 3 million killed by Pakistani forces and Razakar collaborators; international estimates range from 300,000 to 500,000; Pakistani accounts give lower numbers. The International Crimes Tribunal established by Bangladesh (2010) has tried and convicted (including by death) figures from the 1971 period for crimes against humanity — a unique post-conflict justice process 40 years after the events.

laws.title: Digital Security Act 2018 (DSA) & Cyber Repression
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's cybercrime law used against journalists and critics
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Digital Security Act (2018) replaced the Information and Communications Technology Act (ICT Act 2006). The DSA criminalized: propaganda against 'Liberation War' founding ideology, digital content 'distorting the image of the nation', and undefined 'offensive' content. The ICT Act Section 57 had been used against 1,500+ people before DSA replaced it. The DSA was more expansive: journalists, cartoonists, a teacher who complained on Facebook about local corruption, and critics of the government were arrested. Over 1,000 cases filed in the first 3 years. After mass protests by student-led revolution that ousted PM Sheikh Hasina (August 2024), DSA was replaced by the Cyber Security Act (2023) — critics say it retains similar repressive provisions.
laws.penalty: Spreading disinformation about Liberation War: up to 14 years. Publishing content damaging national image: up to 10 years. Hacking: up to 14 years.
