exceptions: Journalistic activities with valid press credentials have some theoretical protection
Academic research on cybersecurity nominally protected
Court-approved security research activities exempt

quiz.q: What political event in August 2024 changed Bangladesh's government and may affect its repressive DSA provisions?
options: Bangladesh held its most democratic election ever, bringing an opposition coalition to power
A student-led mass uprising ousted PM Sheikh Hasina after 15 years in power — she fled to India
A military coup removed the civilian government and suspended all laws
Bangladesh joined ASEAN which required repealing the DSA
quiz.explanation: In July-August 2024, massive student protests (initially against job quotas for descendants of 1971 Liberation War fighters) escalated into a national uprising against Sheikh Hasina's increasingly authoritarian rule. After security forces killed hundreds of protesters, Hasina resigned and fled to India on August 5, 2024. A Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus-led interim government took over. This dramatic political transition creates opportunity to address the DSA's repressive provisions that Hasina's government had used to silence journalists and critics.

laws.title: Bangladesh Labour Act 2006 — Garment Industry and Workers
laws.subtitle: Labor rights in Bangladesh's world-leading garment sector
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Labour Act governs the world's second-largest garment export sector (after China, before Vietnam). The Ready Made Garment (RMG) industry employs 4 million workers (80% women) and generates 85% of Bangladesh's exports ($42B). Rana Plaza collapse (2013): an 8-story garment factory building collapsed killing 1,134 workers — the worst garment industry accident ever. It triggered global reform: Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh (binding safety inspections by international brands) and Alliance for Bangladesh Worker Safety. Minimum wage for garment workers was ৳12,500/month ($113) as of 2023 — workers struck demanding ৳20,000. Trade unions in garment sector remain suppressed.
laws.penalty: Factory safety violations: fines and closure. Child labor in RMG: criminal prosecution. Withholding wages: criminal liability plus triple damages.
exceptions: Export Processing Zones (EPZ) have modified labor law framework — trade unions historically restricted (partially reformed)
Home-based workers in informal production networks have minimal formal protections
Government factories have modified industrial relations framework

quiz.q: What was the Rana Plaza collapse and why did it change global fashion industry practices?
options: A financial scandal in Bangladesh's garment export pricing
The 2013 collapse of an 8-story garment factory killing 1,134 workers — triggering global binding safety inspection agreements
A chemical spill at a textile dyeing factory that contaminated the water supply
A labor strike at Rana Plaza that became a model for union organizing
quiz.explanation: Rana Plaza's collapse on April 24, 2013 — killing 1,134 garment workers — was the deadliest garment industry accident ever. Rescue workers found workers' bodies alongside clothing for Primark, Walmart, and other major Western brands. The disaster forced the global fashion industry to act: the Accord on Fire and Building Safety (binding, with independent inspectors and legal accountability) and the Alliance (voluntary US brands) were created. The Accord later became the International Accord, extending beyond Bangladesh.

laws.title: Bangladesh Climate Change Strategy — World's Most Climate Vulnerable
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's existential climate vulnerability and adaptation
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh is the world's most climate-vulnerable country: two-thirds of the country is less than 5 meters above sea level; it depends on the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna river system's 5-meter annual floods for agricultural fertility; and lies in the Bay of Bengal cyclone track. Sea level rise of 0.5-1m by 2100 could subplace 20+ million people. Bangladesh regularly experiences catastrophic cyclones: 1970 Bhola cyclone killed 300,000-500,000. Bangladesh has dramatically improved cyclone preparedness (1991: 138,000 deaths; 2007 Sidr: 3,400 deaths; better early warning/evacuation). Bangladesh spends 2.5% of GDP on climate adaptation — significant for a low-income country. 'Climate migrants' from river islands (chars) have been resettled.
laws.penalty: Environmental violations in coastal zones: administrative fines. Industrial pollution affecting waterways: criminal prosecution under Environment Act. Land reclamation without EIA: prohibited.
exceptions: Traditional flood-adapted agriculture and aquaculture practices modified from standard environmental regulations
Emergency flood response overrides normal construction permitting
Climate migration assistance programs for displaced coastal communities
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change Bangladesh

quiz.q: What improvements have reduced cyclone death tolls in Bangladesh despite continued climate vulnerability?
options: Bangladesh moved all coastal populations to highland areas since 1991
Early warning systems and pre-positioned cyclone shelters reduced deaths from 138,000 (1991) to 3,400 (2007) for comparable-strength cyclones
Bangladesh built a seawall protecting the entire 200km coastline
Bangladesh receives US military support for cyclone evacuation
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's cyclone death toll reduction is a public health success story: in 1991, Cyclone Bob killed 138,000 people. In 2007, Cyclone Sidr of similar strength killed about 3,400. The dramatic difference reflects: an early warning system reaching coastal villages 72 hours before landfall, 4,000+ concrete cyclone shelters on stilts above flood levels accessible to coastal communities, trained volunteer wardens, and effective evacuation culture. Bangladesh's low-cost cyclone preparedness is studied globally as a model for adaptation under resource constraints.

laws.title: International Crimes Tribunal Act — War Crimes Prosecution
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's prosecution of 1971 Liberation War crimes
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal (ICT, 2010) was established to prosecute crimes during the 1971 Liberation War. Over 50 years after the war, the ICT has tried and convicted leaders of Jamaat-e-Islami (the Islamist party that opposed independence) for genocide, murder, rape, and deportation. Multiple executions occurred. The ICT process was criticized by international legal scholars: insufficient due process protections, inadequate witness protection, and political motivations (the government prosecuted opposition party leaders). The 2024 student revolution raised questions about the tribunal's continuity. Bangladesh's liberation war narrative is politically central — who is a 'Razakar' (traitor/collaborator) was the spark for the student protests.
laws.penalty: Genocide: death penalty or life imprisonment. Crimes against humanity: death or life. War crimes: up to death penalty. Abetting: up to life imprisonment.
exceptions: ICT has jurisdiction only over 1971 war crimes, not subsequent offenses
Individuals who actively fought for independence (Muktijoddha) have exemption
Death penalty convictions subject to presidential mercy petition

quiz.q: What controversial aspect of Bangladesh's ICT war crimes tribunal drew international legal criticism?
options: The tribunal prosecuted Pakistani military officers who are beyond its jurisdiction
International scholars criticized insufficient due process, inadequate witness protection, and the prosecution of opposition political leaders 40+ years after events
The ICT tried and executed people for crimes they were too young to have committed
The tribunal granted blanket immunity to everyone making peace possible
quiz.explanation: While the ICT's goal of accountability for 1971 crimes was broadly supported internationally, its process was criticized: trials proceeded with inadequate rights for defendants, witnesses faced intimidation, transcripts showed troubling interactions between prosecution and judges, and the defendants were primarily leaders of Jamaat-e-Islami — the main opposition coalition partner at the time. The combination of legitimate historical justice and politically convenient prosecutions undermined the tribunal's credibility with international legal observers.

laws.title: Bangladesh Bank Act & Financial Sector Development
laws.subtitle: Central banking and banking sector governance in Bangladesh
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh Bank Act governs the central bank. Bangladesh's banking sector is characterized by high non-performing loans (NPL ratio 8-12%), state bank dominance, and banking scandals. The Bangladesh Bank itself was hacked in 2016: $81 million was stolen through fraudulent SWIFT instructions (routing money to casinos in the Philippines), the biggest bank robbery in history. The incident exposed weaknesses in international banking security. Islami Bank Bangladesh (the country's largest private bank) came under regulatory investigation in 2022. Mobile financial services have transformed Bangladesh: bKash (backed by BRAC and others) has 50M+ users and is one of the world's largest mobile money platforms — transforming financial inclusion for garment workers and rural populations.
laws.penalty: Banking fraud: up to 10 years imprisonment and fines under Money Loan Court Act. Loan default: Commercial Court proceedings for recovery. hundi/hawala: criminalized but widely used for remittances.
exceptions: Non-bank microfinance institutions (Grameen, BRAC, ASA) operate under MRA regulatory framework separate from banking law
Mobile financial services (MFS) licensed separately by Bangladesh Bank
Agent banking networks in rural areas have modified KYC requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Bangladesh Bank — Central Bank of Bangladesh

quiz.q: What was the 2016 Bangladesh Bank cyberheist and how much was stolen?
options: $1 million was stolen when hackers accessed ATM networks
$81 million was stolen through fraudulent SWIFT instructions — the largest bank cyber-robbery in history
$500,000 was stolen from Bangladesh Bank's forex reserves
Bangladesh Bank itself was not hacked — its correspondent in New York was the target only
quiz.explanation: In February 2016, hackers sent fraudulent SWIFT messages from Bangladesh Bank's account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, attempting to transfer $951 million to accounts in the Philippines and Sri Lanka. $81 million reached Philippines casino accounts before the fraud was detected (a spelling error in one instruction — 'fandation' instead of 'foundation' — triggered manual review that stopped most transfers). The heist exposed vulnerabilities in SWIFT's member bank security and led to major global banking security overhauls.

laws.title: Export Processing Zones Act & Garment Export Framework
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's EPZ model and export competitiveness
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Export Processing Zones (EPZ) Act and Bangladesh Export Processing Zones Authority (BEPZA) govern special industrial zones that drive export growth. Bangladesh has 8 EPZs (Chittagong, Dhaka, Comilla, etc.) plus new Special Economic Zones (SEZs). EPZs offer: tax holidays (10 years), duty-free import of machinery and inputs, simplified customs, and historically — no trade unions (partially reformed). Bangladesh has exceptional trade competitiveness: RMG exports ($42B), emerging pharmaceuticals, leather, and jute. Bangladesh graduated from LDC (Least Developed Country) status in 2026 — losing EU GSP benefits that gave duty-free access ('Everything But Arms'). This graduation creates competitive pressure to maintain price competitiveness without trade preferences.
laws.penalty: Operating in EPZ without BEPZA approval: administrative sanctions. Tax fraud on EPZ incentives: recovery plus penalties. Environmental violations in EPZ: Environmental Court proceedings.
exceptions: EPZ companies may not sell in domestic market without BEPZA permission
100% foreign ownership permitted in EPZ — no local equity requirement
EPZ workers have BEPZA-administered disputes resolution rather than standard labor court system

quiz.q: What trade challenge does Bangladesh face after 'graduating' from Least Developed Country status?
options: Bangladesh must repay all development aid received as an LDC
Losing EU GSP duty-free preferences ('Everything But Arms') — forcing Bangladesh to compete without preferential tariff access
Bangladesh must adopt EU labor and environmental standards as a condition of graduation
Bangladesh becomes ineligible for IMF concessional lending after LDC graduation
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's LDC graduation (expected 2026) means losing the EU's 'Everything But Arms' preferential tariff arrangement, which gave duty-free, quota-free access to EU markets for all exports. Without EBA, Bangladesh's garments face standard EU tariffs of ~12% — reducing price competitiveness against countries with EU free trade agreements (Vietnam has EVFTA). Bangladesh is negotiating for enhanced GSP+ status and lobbying for extended transition periods. This graduation paradox — reward for development success creates new economic vulnerability — affects multiple countries.

laws.title: Bangladesh National Health Policy & Pharmaceutical Sector
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's TRIPS waiver and generic medicine production
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh has a unique global pharmaceutical position: as an LDC, Bangladesh had TRIPS Agreement exemptions allowing it to manufacture generic versions of patented medicines without licenses. Bangladesh's pharmaceutical sector exports generic medicines globally. After LDC graduation, Bangladesh faces TRIPS obligations that would require licensing patented medicines. Bangladesh's healthcare outcomes are remarkable for its income level: life expectancy of 73 years (comparable to much richer nations), declining maternal mortality (176/100,000, one of Asia's fastest declines), and strong childhood vaccination rates. BRAC's community health worker program is studied globally. Bangladesh spends only ~3% of GDP on health.
laws.penalty: Manufacturing counterfeit medicines: criminal prosecution. Operating pharmacy without license: administrative closure. Medical malpractice: civil and criminal liability.
exceptions: As LDC, Bangladesh exempted from pharmaceutical patent protections (until 2026 graduation)
Traditional herbal medicines regulated under separate framework
Government health programs distributing essential medicines are exempt from normal pricing restrictions
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare Bangladesh

quiz.q: What intellectual property advantage did Bangladesh have as an LDC that may change after 2026?
options: Bangladesh could patent indigenous traditional knowledge without paying royalties
As an LDC, Bangladesh could manufacture generic versions of patented medicines without licensing — potentially changing after LDC graduation
Bangladesh received free technology transfers from developed countries under LDC provisions
Bangladesh was exempt from all WTO intellectual property requirements indefinitely
quiz.explanation: The TRIPS Agreement's LDC exception allowed Bangladesh to produce generic versions of patented pharmaceuticals without paying licensing fees — enabling a thriving generic medicine industry exporting affordable drugs globally. After graduating from LDC status, Bangladesh must comply with full TRIPS pharmaceutical patent protections, which could require paying royalties to multinational pharma companies. Bangladesh negotiated for a transition period, but this LDC graduation 'cost' is a significant policy challenge for the pharmaceutical sector.

laws.title: Land Reform in Bangladesh — Vested Property and Minority Rights
laws.subtitle: Land dispossession of religious minorities in Bangladesh
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh has a persistent problem of land dispossession of its Hindu minority (8% of population). The Enemy/Vested Property Act (originally 1965 Pakistani law, retained post-independence) designated Hindu-owned properties as 'vested property' subject to government acquisition if the owner 'absented' — effectively penalizing migration to India. An estimated 2.6 million acres of Hindu minority land was confiscated or occupied under this law. The Vested Property Return Act (2001) partially addressed this but implementation has been very slow. Hindu communities in Bangladesh regularly report land grabbing, intimidation, and property destruction — particularly during political upheavals and communal violence episodes.
laws.penalty: Land fraud (fake documents, intimidation of minorities): criminal prosecution, but enforcement weak for powerful perpetrators. Vested property illegal occupiers: eviction orders under Vested Property Return Act.
exceptions: Non-resident Bangladeshis may hold property with proper registration — including overseas migrants
Vested Property Return Board can restore confiscated properties to original owners or heirs
Tribal minority communities in Chittagong Hill Tracts have modified land rights under CHT Peace Accord
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Law Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Bangladesh

quiz.q: What colonial-era law was retained in Bangladesh that led to dispossession of Hindu minority land?
options: The Hindu Succession Act that denied women the right to inherit land
The Enemy/Vested Property Act (1965) designating Hindu-owned properties as 'vested property' if owners migrated to India
The Zamindar Abolition Act that stripped Hindu landlords of all land
The Muslim Family Laws Ordinance applied to Hindu families
quiz.explanation: The Enemy Property (Custodian) Act was enacted in 1965 by Pakistan, designating as 'enemy property' any assets belonging to those who moved to India (then enemy state). After Bangladesh's independence, the law was retained as 'Vested Property'. Any Hindu who migrated to India — whether before or after independence — had their Bangladesh properties seized. This led to massive land confiscation from Bangladesh's Hindu minority, estimated at 2.6 million acres. The law was not formally repealed until 2001 and return of property has been extremely slow.

laws.title: Terrorism Act & Extremism in Bangladesh
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's battle against militant Islamism
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Anti-Terrorism Act (2009) criminalizes terrorist organizations and financing. Bangladesh has experienced domestic Islamist terrorism: Holey Artisan Bakery attack (Dhaka, 2016) — ISIS-affiliated attackers killed 22 people (20 foreigners) in an upscale restaurant. The Jamaat-ul-Mujahideen Bangladesh (JMB) and Ansar al Islam have been designated terrorist organizations. Bangladesh has been reasonably effective at counter-terrorism: intelligence-led operations, community engagement, and deradicalization. The country's secular founding ideology and majority moderate Muslim population have been bulwarks against extremism, though economic pressures and political manipulation have sometimes fed radical recruitment. Madrasa education reform and addressing youth unemployment are key prevention strategies.
laws.penalty: Terrorist act causing death: life imprisonment to death. Joining terrorist organization: up to 10 years. Financing terrorism: up to 10 years.
exceptions: Religious education in madrasas is constitutionally protected
Legitimate Islamic charities with proper registration may operate without terrorism suspicion
Political parties with Islamic ideology (Islami Oikya Jote etc.) are legal if they do not advocate violence

quiz.q: What 2016 terrorist attack in Dhaka raised international alarm about extremism in Bangladesh?
options: A suicide bombing at a government ministry building killing 50 officials
The Holey Artisan Bakery attack by ISIS-affiliated militants killing 22 people (20 foreigners) in an upscale restaurant
A series of blog editor murders by Islamist groups targeting atheist writers
A simultaneous bombing of 500 country-wide sites by Jamaatut Mujahideen Bangladesh
quiz.explanation: The July 2016 Holey Artisan Bakery attack in Dhaka's diplomatic Gulshan area shocked Bangladesh and the world: ISIS-affiliated Bangladeshi attackers took hostages and killed 22 people, primarily foreigners (Italian, Japanese) who could not recite the Quran. The attack demonstrated that ISIS had recruited educated Bangladeshis from elite backgrounds — not just the poor and marginalized. It shattered the narrative that Bangladesh's moderate Islam was immune to international jihadi influence and triggered major counter-terrorism reforms.

laws.title: Acid Violence and Acid Control Act 2002 — Bangladesh
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's legal response to acid attack epidemic
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh enacted the Acid Offences Prevention Act and Acid Control Act in 2002 following an epidemic of acid attacks, primarily against women and girls who refused marriage proposals or demands for dowry. Bangladesh had among the world's highest rates of acid violence: over 400 attacks annually in the early 2000s. The laws introduced the death penalty for acid attacks causing death and 14 years minimum for causing grievous hurt. Crucially, the Acid Control Act restricted acid sales — purchasers required licenses and sellers required registers. This supply-side intervention dramatically reduced attacks: from 400+ annually to under 100 by 2010. Bangladesh's experience is studied globally as a model for controlling acid violence through supply restriction rather than solely through increased penalties.
laws.penalty: Acid attack causing death: death penalty. Causing grievous hurt with acid: 14 years to life. Illegal acid sale: up to 3 years and fine. Failure to register acid purchases: administrative penalty.
exceptions: Industrial users of acid (battery manufacturers, metal industries) have bulk licensing with different registration requirements
Medical and laboratory grade acids regulated under separate pharmaceutical and chemical safety frameworks
Import of acid for industrial purposes requires separate import licensing from Commerce Ministry

quiz.q: How did Bangladesh reduce acid attacks from 400+ annually to under 100 by restricting what?
options: Bangladesh reduced attacks by executing convicted acid attackers as a deterrent
Supply-side restriction — requiring licenses to purchase acid and registers for sales — dramatically cut attack rates, complementing criminal penalties
Bangladesh banned all acid nationwide including industrial uses
Bangladesh introduced a mandatory 72-hour waiting period before acid could be purchased
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's acid attack reduction resulted primarily from supply-side control: the Acid Control Act 2002 required buyers to have licenses and sellers to maintain purchase registers, making acid harder to obtain impulsively. Acid attacks are often crimes of passion or revenge — reducing impulsive access to the tool reduced incidents. This supply-side approach, combined with criminal penalties and a survivor support network, reduced attacks by 75%+. The Bangladesh model is cited by UNICEF, WHO, and advocacy organizations as a replicable approach to acid violence reduction.

laws.title: Prevention of Oppression Against Women and Children Act 2000
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's laws against violence against women and children
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Prevention of Oppression Against Women and Children Act 2000 (Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain) consolidated laws against rape, trafficking, dowry violence, and acid attacks. Bangladesh has significant gender-based violence challenges: official statistics show 300+ rapes reported monthly, with actual incidence far higher. Dowry demands and violence remain common despite prohibition. The 2020 amendment introduced the death penalty for rape (previously 14 years max). Child marriage is another challenge: Bangladesh has the world's 4th highest child marriage rate — 59% of girls married before 18 (2017 data). The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 was criticized for including an 'exceptional circumstance' clause allowing child marriage in some cases.
laws.penalty: Rape: death penalty (2020 amendment). Dowry death: death penalty. Trafficking of women: death penalty or life. Child marriage below 18: up to 2 years. Dowry demand: up to 5 years.
exceptions: 'Exceptional circumstances' clause in Child Marriage Restraint Act permits court-authorized child marriages in unspecified circumstances
Government schemes for early marriage registration of minor pregnancy are a contested area
Sharia-influenced personal law applies to Muslim inheritance and family matters
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Women and Children Affairs Bangladesh

quiz.q: Why was Bangladesh's Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 criticized despite setting 18 as the minimum marriage age?
options: The law reduced the minimum age from 21 to 18
The 'exceptional circumstances' clause allows court-authorized child marriages with no specified minimum age, creating a loophole
The law failed to include any penalty for parents who arrange child marriages
Bangladesh set 18 as the age for boys but kept the girls' age at 16
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's 2017 Child Marriage Restraint Act was criticized for an 'exceptional circumstances' clause that permits courts to authorize child marriages without a specified minimum age when parents and a court agree circumstances justify it. UNICEF, Human Rights Watch, and women's organizations called this a dangerous loophole that could institutionalize child marriage under judicial cover. The clause was reportedly added under pressure from religious groups and MPs from rural areas with high child marriage rates, undermining the law's stated goal of eliminating child marriage.

laws.title: Forest Act and Deforestation in Bangladesh
laws.subtitle: Forest protection in one of the world's most densely populated countries
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Forest Act governs forest conservation in a country with severe deforestation pressure. Bangladesh has only 11% forest cover (against recommended 25%), concentrated in the Sundarbans (world's largest mangrove forest, 10,000 km², shared with India) and Chittagong Hill Tracts. The Sundarbans provide critical cyclone protection: the 2007 Sidr cyclone — which would have killed hundreds of thousands without the Sundarbans barrier — caused only 3,400 deaths partly because the mangroves absorbed storm surge. The Sundarbans is threatened by sea level rise and the Rampal coal power plant built near its edge. Deforestation continues in Chittagong Hill Tracts driven by Bengali settler migration. Bangladesh also faces severe industrial pollution of rivers including the Buriganga (heavily polluted by Dhaka industries).
laws.penalty: Illegal tree cutting in reserved forest: up to 2 years and fine. Wildlife poaching in forest: up to 3 years. Industrial pollution of forest waterways: environmental court proceedings.
exceptions: Indigenous communities in Chittagong Hill Tracts have traditional forest use rights under CHT Accord
Sundarbans fishing communities have regulated access for traditional fishing and honey collecting
Emergency construction in flood-protection zones may use forest materials with departmental permission

quiz.q: How did the Sundarbans mangrove forest help protect Bangladesh during Cyclone Sidr in 2007?
options: The Sundarbans were completely destroyed by Sidr but were later replanted
The Sundarbans absorbed storm surge and reduced wind speeds — contributing to far fewer deaths than a comparable cyclone caused in 1991 without similar forest protection
The Sundarbans have no protection value — cyclone shelters saved lives
Sidr missed the Sundarbans entirely and hit unpopulated areas
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's 1991 cyclone killed 138,000 people; 2007 Cyclone Sidr of comparable intensity killed about 3,400. The Sundarbans mangroves played a significant protective role: mangroves reduce storm surge height, slow cyclone intensity, and provide wind barriers. The World Bank and IUCN studied the Sidr event as evidence of mangrove natural disaster protection value. Bangladesh's coastal protection plans explicitly incorporate Sundarbans conservation as infrastructure — the mangroves are recognized as a 'green shield' against cyclones.

laws.title: Rohingya Refugee Crisis — Bangladesh
laws.subtitle: World's largest refugee influx and Bangladesh's response
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh hosts approximately 1 million Rohingya refugees in Cox's Bazar (world's largest refugee camp, Kutupalong), following the 2017 Myanmar military crackdown. The Rohingya are a Muslim minority from Rakhine State, Myanmar, denied citizenship by Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law. The 2017 military offensive — described as 'genocide' by a UN fact-finding mission — drove 700,000+ Rohingya into Bangladesh in weeks. Bangladesh faces enormous strain: environmental destruction around camps, crime, trafficking, and disease risks. Bangladesh has been extremely generous in accepting refugees despite being a poor, densely populated country. Repatriation to Myanmar has not occurred (Rohingya refuse without safety guarantees; Myanmar denies responsibility).
laws.penalty: Rohingya refugees formally lack legal status in Bangladesh — Bangladesh not party to 1951 Refugee Convention. Working outside camp is technically illegal. Moving freely is restricted.
exceptions: UNHCR registration provides some protection from deportation despite Bangladesh's non-Convention status
NGOs operating in camps under government coordination framework
Bangladesh allows limited movement for medical treatment and essential services
laws.sourceLabel: Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner Bangladesh

quiz.q: Why is the Rohingya refugee situation particularly difficult to resolve through repatriation?
options: Bangladesh refuses to allow any Rohingya to return to Myanmar under any circumstances
The Rohingya refuse to return without safety guarantees and citizenship rights — which Myanmar denies, claiming Rohingya are not Burmese citizens
Rohingya have all been permanently resettled in third countries and cannot return
Myanmar has offered full citizenship to Rohingya but they prefer staying in Bangladesh
quiz.explanation: Rohingya repatriation faces a fundamental impasse: Rohingya refugees refuse to return without guarantees of safety, freedom of movement, and citizenship — which Myanmar's government refuses to provide. Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law excludes Rohingya from 135 recognized ethnic groups. Multiple voluntary repatriation attempts since 2017 have had zero or near-zero departures because Rohingya distrust Myanmar's assurances. This creates a protracted refugee situation with Bangladesh — a poor, densely populated country — hosting 1 million people indefinitely.

laws.title: Income Tax Act Bangladesh & Tax Policy
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's tax collection challenges and informal economy
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's National Board of Revenue (NBR) administers income tax, VAT, and customs under an outdated Income Tax Ordinance (1984, now being replaced by Income Tax Act 2023). Bangladesh has very low tax-to-GDP ratio: 7-9% (one of the world's lowest), compared to the 15% threshold considered minimum for development financing. The informal economy represents 80%+ of employment. Tax compliance is low: only 3-4 million tax returns filed in a country of 170 million. Bangladesh relies heavily on customs duties and VAT rather than income tax. The tax system is complex, with numerous exemptions and discretionary decisions creating corruption opportunities. Bangladesh has repeatedly missed IMF revenue mobilization targets.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: up to 3 years imprisonment and triple the evaded tax. VAT fraud: administrative penalties and prosecution. Smuggling: up to 20 years for serious offenses.
exceptions: EPZ companies have tax holidays for 10 years
NGOs with tax exemption certificates on foreign donations exempt from income tax
Cottage and micro industries below threshold exempt from corporate income tax

quiz.q: What is Bangladesh's tax-to-GDP ratio and why does this matter for development?
options: Bangladesh collects 25% of GDP in taxes — comparable to European welfare states
Bangladesh's 7-9% tax-to-GDP ratio is one of the world's lowest — below the 15% threshold economists consider the minimum for development financing
Bangladesh has a negative tax-to-GDP ratio because it spends more on tax exemptions than it collects
Bangladesh does not collect taxes — it relies entirely on foreign aid and remittances
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's tax-to-GDP ratio of 7-9% is critically low. The IMF and World Bank cite 15% as the minimum for a country to finance development (education, health, infrastructure) independently. Bangladesh's low ratio means it is heavily dependent on development aid and external borrowing. The low ratio reflects high informal economy (where income is invisible to tax authorities), weak enforcement, political resistance to taxing wealthy elites, and numerous exemptions. IMF programs have repeatedly required Bangladesh to raise tax collection as a condition of support.

laws.title: National Digital Bangladesh Policy & ICT Sector
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's digital transformation and tech industry growth
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Digital Bangladesh vision (2009) drove rapid ICT development. Bangladesh has 180M+ mobile subscribers (SIM penetration 100%+), 120M+ internet users, and thriving mobile financial services (bKash, Nagad with 50M+ users each). The ICT sector has grown: Bangladesh is a significant software export destination (NASSCOM ranks Bangladesh IT firms). The IT Enabled Services (ITES) sector employs 650,000. Bangladesh has significant freelancing community (2nd globally in freelancing platforms per capita). However, digital infrastructure disparities remain: rural broadband coverage is limited. Cybersecurity frameworks are developing. The Digital Security Act's repressive application has conflicted with the otherwise positive digital development agenda.
laws.penalty: Software piracy: civil damages and criminal prosecution. Cybercrime: DSA provisions. Digital fraud: up to 5 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Open source software use in government is actively encouraged with modified procurement rules
Startups in designated tech parks (Software Technology Park, BEZA ICT parks) receive tax holidays
Digital payment systems integrating MFS need Bank Bangladesh and BTRC dual licensing

quiz.q: What is Bangladesh's unique position in global freelancing?
options: Bangladesh banned freelancing as a form of tax evasion
Bangladesh ranks 2nd globally in freelancing platform participation per capita — a significant digital economy achievement
Bangladesh produced the world's most valuable tech startup (worth $50B+)
Bangladesh trained all government workers as freelancers
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh has one of the world's largest freelancer communities relative to its population, ranking 2nd globally on major platforms like Upwork and Freelancer. Hundreds of thousands of Bangladeshis earn foreign currency through digital work (graphics design, web development, data entry, digital marketing). This remote work revolution has created income opportunities beyond the garment sector, particularly for educated youth. The government actively supports freelancing through training programs and simplified banking channels for receiving foreign payments.

laws.title: Child Rights Act & Juvenile Justice in Bangladesh
laws.subtitle: Child protection laws and child rights enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's Children Act (2013) consolidated child rights protections and established child-friendly justice system. Bangladesh ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1990). Child labor remains significant: 1.2 million children in hazardous work despite prohibition. The garment industry theoretically prohibits child labor following international pressure post-Rana Plaza — compliance has improved significantly in formal factories. Informal supply chains have more child labor. Street children in Dhaka (estimated 500,000+) face exploitation, violence, and lack of access to services. Child marriage remains at 59% under-18 despite legal prohibition. Bangladesh has 1 child development center (reformatory) per division — grossly insufficient for child justice needs.
laws.penalty: Child labor in hazardous work: employers prosecuted under Labour Act. Sexual abuse of child: up to death penalty under Nari O Shishu Act. Child marriage arranging: up to 2 years parents/guardians.
exceptions: Children 12-16 may do light non-hazardous work outside school hours with parental consent
Family agricultural work is exempted from child labor prohibitions
Court-ordered diversion programs for minor offenders under 18 are preferred over prosecution
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Women and Children Affairs Bangladesh

quiz.q: Despite Bangladesh's child labor prohibition, how many children remain in hazardous work?
options: Zero — Bangladesh has completely eliminated child labor
About 1.2 million children remain in hazardous work despite legal prohibitions and international pressure
About 50,000 children — mostly concentrated in specific districts
Over 10 million children — more than any other country
quiz.explanation: Despite legal prohibitions and significant international pressure (particularly after Rana Plaza), approximately 1.2 million Bangladeshi children remain in hazardous work. Formal garment factories have largely eliminated child labor under international buyer pressure, but informal supply chains, construction, domestic work, brick kilns, and ship-breaking yards still employ children in dangerous conditions. Enforcement is difficult given the scale of informality and economic pressure on poor families. Bangladesh's high child marriage rate (59% under-18) also affects girls' labor market participation and education.

laws.title: Ship-breaking Industry and Maritime Law Bangladesh
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's dangerous ship recycling industry
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh is one of the world's top 3 ship-breaking countries (with India and Pakistan), recycling 200+ ships annually at Chittagong's ship-breaking yards. The industry recovers valuable steel (meeting 20% of Bangladesh's steel demand), but working conditions are extremely dangerous: workers manually cut apart ships containing asbestos, lead, mercury, oil sludge, and other hazardous materials with minimal protection. Child labor was prevalent. Worker deaths are frequent: estimated 1 per week. International campaigns led to the Basel Convention's application to ships (Hong Kong International Convention for Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships). Bangladesh has ship recycling yards at Sitakunda, Chittagong — attempting to comply with international standards while remaining cost-competitive.
laws.penalty: Unsafe working conditions: Factory Act penalties, criminal prosecution for deaths due to negligence. Importing ships with banned toxic materials: environmental and customs penalties. Child labor in ship-breaking: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Certified 'green' recycling yards complying with Hong Kong Convention standards may import ships categorized as hazardous waste under Basel exemption
Structural steel recovered is exempted from quality standards requiring import documentation
Emergency recycling of government naval vessels may have modified environmental requirements

quiz.q: Why is Bangladesh's ship-breaking industry controversial despite its economic value?
options: Ship-breaking is controversial because it competes with Japanese and South Korean shipbuilding industries
Workers manually dismantle ships containing asbestos, lead, mercury, and oil sludge with minimal protection — resulting in frequent deaths and toxic contamination
Ship-breaking is controversial because Bangladesh exports the recycled steel rather than using it domestically
The industry is controversial because it only employs foreign workers rather than Bangladeshis
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's ship-breaking yards at Sitakunda, Chittagong, are among the world's most dangerous industrial workplaces: workers use cutting torches to manually dismember ships on tidal beaches without protection from asbestos, toxic chemicals, or structural hazards. Ship fires, explosions, and toxic exposure cause frequent deaths (estimated 1 per week across the industry). Environmental contamination of the Chittagong coastline is severe. International NGOs (Shipbreaking Platform) campaign for conversion to environmentally sound 'green recycling' with enclosed facilities and worker protections.

laws.title: Local Government Act Bangladesh — Union Parishad System
laws.subtitle: Decentralized governance and local democracy in Bangladesh
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh's local government operates through a tiered system: Union Parishad (UP) at the village level, Upazila Parishad at sub-district level, Zila Parishad at district level, and City Corporations/Pourashavas for urban areas. The Union Parishad — covering 5,000-10,000 people — is the closest government to rural Bangladeshis. Women's representation in UPs has been enhanced: 33% reserved seats for women members. However, Union Parishad chairmen (still predominantly male) often dominate proceedings. The salish (village arbitration) system operated informally through UP and community elders — sometimes imposing extrajudicial punishments including fatwas against women for alleged moral violations. Government has prosecuted illegal fatwas under criminal law.
laws.penalty: Imposing unlawful fatwas with physical punishment: criminal prosecution of all participants. Obstruction of official UP functions: administrative and criminal penalties. Electoral fraud in local elections: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Salish informal arbitration for civil disputes is tolerated and used to reduce court burden
Village courts (operating under Village Courts Act 2006) can adjudicate minor cases up to Tk75,000
Union Parishad members have immunity from civil suits for official actions

quiz.q: What informal extrajudicial practice in Bangladesh's village communities has been criminalized under central government law?
options: Village elders holding informal arbitration sessions (salish) for property disputes
Fatwas imposing physical punishment on women issued by local religious figures — which Bangladesh's courts have prosecuted participants for
Traditional healing practices by village doctors that conflict with modern medicine
Dowry negotiation before marriage which is conducted informally outside legal registration
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's courts have prosecuted cases where village fatwas ordered physical punishment — typically flogging or '101 lashes' — of women accused of adultery, refusing arranged marriages, or other 'moral violations'. Multiple high-profile cases where women died after fatwa-ordered beatings were prosecuted as criminal assault and manslaughter. Bangladesh's Supreme Court declared fatwas imposing punishment to be illegal. However, enforcement is difficult in rural areas where local religious authority may override formal legal institutions.

laws.title: Drug Control Ordinance & Maternal Health Progress Bangladesh
laws.subtitle: Bangladesh's dramatic health improvements: maternal mortality and vaccination
laws.fullDescription: Bangladesh has achieved remarkable health outcomes at low income levels: maternal mortality reduced from 574/100,000 (1990) to 163/100,000 (2020); child vaccination coverage 97%+; life expectancy 73 years. These achievements came through community health workers (community-based skilled birth attendants), BRAC's health programs, and NGO-delivered healthcare. Bangladesh's Drug Control Ordinance (1982) established the National Drug Policy — a model followed by other developing countries for regulating drug prices and essential medicines. Bangladesh required drug companies to prove essential medicines were available at affordable prices. The pharmaceutical industry grew under this framework to 97% domestic self-sufficiency — Bangladesh manufactures nearly all medicines it needs.
laws.penalty: Manufacturing or selling counterfeit medicines: up to 5 years imprisonment and fines. Drug trafficking: up to life imprisonment. Unlicensed medical practice: up to 2 years.
exceptions: Essential medicines on National Essential Medicines List have price controls
Diplomatic missions may import foreign medicines for personal use without registration
Clinical trial medications operate under separate Drug Administration oversight
laws.sourceLabel: Directorate General of Drug Administration Bangladesh

quiz.q: How did Bangladesh achieve 97% domestic pharmaceutical self-sufficiency?
options: Bangladesh received a US pharmaceutical factory as foreign aid in the 1980s
The 1982 National Drug Policy — restricting which medicines could be imported and requiring domestic production — built a pharmaceutical industry achieving near-complete self-sufficiency
Bangladesh's large population attracted all major pharmaceutical companies to build factories
Bangladesh copied drug manufacturing technology from India without licensing fees
quiz.explanation: Bangladesh's 1982 National Drug Policy, modeled partly on ideas from the Brundtland Commission, restricted imports of medicines that could be produced domestically and focused resources on essential medicines. By requiring domestic production and limiting imports, Bangladesh created the conditions for its pharmaceutical industry to develop. Combined with its later TRIPS LDC exemptions (allowing generic manufacturing), Bangladesh built an industry that now supplies 97% of domestic medicine needs and exports generics globally. The policy is studied as a model for pharmaceutical development in low-income countries.
